evidence.label: Canonical ampleness of compact hyperbolic Kähler manifolds

headline: Compact Kähler manifolds with no entire curves have ample canonical bundle, as Kobayashi conjectured.
scope: Compact connected Kähler manifolds of positive dimension in which every holomorphic map from the complex plane is constant.
plain: A complex space is hyperbolic when every holomorphic map from the whole complex plane into it is constant. Kobayashi conjectured that compact hyperbolic Kähler manifolds have an ample canonical bundle. This paper claims to prove that in every positive dimension. A consequence is that such a manifold can be described by polynomial equations in projective space. Earlier proofs needed an extra assumption of negative curvature.
doesNot: This does not address singular spaces, non-Kähler manifolds, or the converse direction from ampleness to hyperbolicity.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: D. Wu and S.-T. Yau, under negative holomorphic sectional curvature
scorecard.significanceWhy: If correct, it settles a central conjecture of complex hyperbolic geometry in the smooth compact Kähler setting.

explanation:
Start with closed surfaces, counted by their holes. A sphere has none, a doughnut has one, and a pretzel shape has two. Each can be given a complex structure, which makes it a compact Riemann surface. On such a surface one can ask about entire curves. An entire curve is a non-constant smooth complex map from the whole complex plane into the surface.

The sphere and the doughnut both receive entire curves. The plane wraps onto the doughnut by rolling it up in two directions. Surfaces with two or more holes receive none. Every such map from the plane is constant. A space with no entire curves is called hyperbolic.

There is a second test. Each surface carries a canonical bundle, the line bundle built from its holomorphic one-forms. Its degree is 2g − 2, where g counts the holes. That gives −2 for the sphere, 0 for the doughnut, and 2 for two holes. Three holes give 4. The bundle is ample, a strong algebraic kind of positivity, exactly when the degree is positive. So among curves, the two tests agree. No entire curves happens exactly when the canonical bundle is ample.

Kobayashi’s canonical-ampleness conjecture asks for one direction of this match in every dimension. Take a compact Kähler manifold, a compact complex space with a compatible way to measure lengths. If it has no entire curves, its canonical bundle should be ample[3]. Ample means some power of the bundle has enough sections to embed the space in projective space. So the conjecture links a ban on maps from the plane to positivity and to being described by polynomial equations[3].

This paper claims to prove the conjecture in every positive dimension[2]. If every holomorphic map from the plane is constant, the canonical bundle is ample. In particular the manifold is projective, meaning it sits inside a complex projective space[2].

Earlier results needed an extra curvature assumption. Wu and Yau showed in 2016 that negative holomorphic sectional curvature forces canonical ampleness on projective manifolds[4]. Tosatti and Yang removed the projectivity assumption in 2017[5]. Diverio and Trapani allowed curvature that is only quasi-negative[6]. Chen and Yang proved ampleness under Gromov’s Kähler hyperbolicity, a different condition[7]. The paper notes that these metric assumptions give curvature inequalities that the absence of entire curves alone does not supply[8].

A weaker conclusion was already known. Ou, and Cao and Höring, showed the canonical bundle is nef when there are no rational curves[9]. Nef is a borderline form of positivity. The remaining issue for ampleness is positive canonical volume[10]. Volume here is a number measuring how much positivity the bundle has in total.

The obstacle is that hyperbolicity gives no curvature at all. It only bounds how fast a holomorphic disc can stretch at its centre[17]. The paper works with extremal discs, maps of the unit disc that maximise a chosen quantity. The hard part sits at the disc’s boundary circle. There, the usual limit arguments do not justify varying an integral over the whole disc[11]. The paper first shows enough regularity at the boundary. It then builds holomorphic families of discs with a fixed centre. One second-derivative identity from these families then gives two positivity estimates[12]. One estimate gives a uniform lower bound on volume. A limit then gives positive top self-intersection of the canonical class[13]. Standard theorems turn that into bigness, projectivity and ampleness.

The paper also claims two consequences. Let n be the dimension. Every power of the canonical bundle of order n + 2 or more is generated by its sections[14]. In dimension 2, that means every power from 4 upward. This step uses a separate OpenAI preprint on Fujita freeness. The second describes a finite cover when the universal cover has a semialgebraic form[15]. It uses another OpenAI preprint. Neither is used in the proof of the main theorem[16].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the analytic disc argument holds. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. The two consequences also rely on other OpenAI preprints.

glossary.meaning: A non-constant holomorphic map from the whole complex plane into a space.
Here: a space into which every holomorphic map from the complex plane is constant.
The line bundle built from a complex manifold's top-degree holomorphic forms.
A positivity property: some power of the bundle has enough sections to embed the space in projective space.
A complex manifold with a compatible way to measure lengths and areas.
Describable by polynomial equations inside a complex projective space.
A borderline form of positivity, weaker than ample.
